definition: In the field of translation, a translation unit is a segment of a text which the translator treats as a single cognitive unit for the purposes of establishing an equivalence.
details: It may be a single word, a phrase, one or more sentences, or even a larger unit. When a translator segments a text into translation units, the larger these units are, the better chance there is of obtaining an idiomatic translation. This is true not only of human translation, but also where human translators use computer-assisted translation, such as translation memories, and when translations are performed by machine translation systems.

explainer.lead: A translation unit is a segment of text a translator treats as a single cognitive unit when establishing equivalence; it may be a word, phrase, one or more sentences, or larger. It matters because larger units give a better chance of an idiomatic translation.

tiers.eli5: It is the chunk of text you handle in one go — sometimes a word, sometimes a whole sentence — rather than always going word by word.
tiers.practitioner: The choice of unit size shapes output quality in human translation, in computer-assisted translation such as translation memories, and in machine translation. The pitfall is choosing units too small, which reduces the chance of an idiomatic result.
tiers.paperLevel: A segment of text treated as a single cognitive unit for establishing equivalence; it may be a single word, a phrase, one or more sentences, or a larger unit. The larger the units, the better the chance of an idiomatic translation, in human and machine translation alike.

explainer.example: A translator treats a full sentence as one unit rather than translating it word by word, improving the chance the result sounds idiomatic.
